Practise Under Pressure

A practice match isn't a tournament. What the research says about practising under pressure, and how to add it to your tennis or padel training safely.

Amir Ardekanian · 3 min read · November 2026

📲This article is also in the appAA Performance · opens without an accountOpen →

A practice match isn't a tournament. You know it, and your body knows it.

The stakes are lower, so the nerves are lower. That's fine while you're learning. But it means practice can't fully show you how you'll play when it counts.

So pressure needs its own practice. Here's what the research says about practising under pressure, and how to add some to your training in tennis or padel. It follows on from The Practice Ladder.

What pressure does to a good shot

When the score matters, the shot you trust can disappear. Researchers don't agree on exactly why.

The research

One idea says you start thinking about your technique. Another says you start worrying about the result. In one study, 70 expert athletes described what they focused on in high-pressure competition. Often it was worries. Hardly ever the movement itself.

So there are two jobs. Make the shot solid enough to survive, and learn to handle the worry that comes with the score.

Pressure can be practised

The research

A 2021 review pooled 14 studies of practising under simulated pressure, ten of them in sport. It improved performance under pressure by a medium amount, for beginners and experienced performers, on open and closed tasks. The authors' advice: build pressure into training instead of just doing more training.

In one experiment, 17 expert basketball players practised free throws for five weeks, some with anxiety added and some without. Only the ones who trained with anxiety kept their accuracy when the pressure went up at the end. A second experiment with expert dart players, throwing from high up on a climbing wall, found the same.

Those were free throws and darts, not rallies. I couldn't find this study done with tennis players. But the result held across very different tasks.

Why a practice match isn't enough

Even a tough practice match isn't the same as competition.

The research

Padel research from Finland compared high-level men's practice matches played under pressure with official competition. Over 4,417 points in 38 matches, winners and errors looked about the same. A separate small study of 10 players found more body tension and more self-confidence before competition than before practice matches.

So a practice match can copy how you play. It can't fully copy how competition feels. That's why competition is its own step on the ladder.

How to add pressure

Add pressure to a skill that already holds when you're calm. Start small.

Pressure comes from consequences. Here are some ways to add them.

  • Keep score, and start games from a tight score like 30-40.
  • Play for something small, like the loser collecting the balls.
  • Play with someone watching, or film the session.
  • Give yourself one serve, with no second.
  • Start the session with a tie-break.
My rule

Add one pressure at a time. If the shot falls apart, you added too much. Drop back one.

Pressure is a dose

Pressure can help or hurt. Australia's sport science body made that point in a 2026 position statement. It says pressure training has to be delivered with care because it can affect an athlete's wellbeing, ideally with a sport psychologist.

So keep it small and short. If you start to dread the session, you've added too much.

Where pressure goes on the ladder

Pressure belongs on the top steps: practice points and practice matches. Competition then adds the real thing. The early steps stay calm on purpose, because that's where you build the shot.

Rule

Make the shot solid when things are calm. Then practise it when they aren't.

Based on Oudejans et al. (2011), Low et al. (2021), Oudejans and Pijpers (2009), Conde-Ripoll et al. (2024, 2025) and Schweickle et al. (2026).
